books.section: The Rise of the Middle Class

stimulus.text: The image shows a Remington Standard typewriter of 1890: a heavy black machine with round keys arranged in rows, a roller at the top for holding paper, and a ruler marked with numbers across the middle. A small plate above the roller reads, in part, “Keep machine free from dust.”
stimulus.source_note: Remington Standard typewriter, 1890. Public domain image from Wikimedia Commons; viewed by the writer.

options.text: A steam locomotive used to haul heavy freight cars
options.misconception: The image shows a small office machine, not a locomotive.

options.text: A large printing press used to print newspapers in a city shop
options.misconception: A press prints whole pages; this machine has keys for typing letters.

options.text: A typewriter, with round keys, a paper roller, and a numbered ruler
A telegraph key used to send messages by wire
options.misconception: A telegraph key is a single lever; this machine has rows of letter keys.

rationales.A: Nothing in the image runs on rails or hauls freight. Look at the keys and the paper roller.
rationales.B: A printing press is far larger and has no letter keys. The rows of round keys mark this as a typewriter.
rationales.C: The round keys in rows, the roller at the top for paper, and the numbered ruler across the middle are the parts of a typewriter.
rationales.D: A telegraph key sends dots and dashes with one lever. This machine types letters with many keys.
rationales.general:
Name what you can see before you reason about it.
1. Look at the front: rows of round keys marked with letters.
2. Look at the top: a roller that holds paper.
3. Look at the middle: a ruler marked with numbers.
4. Keys plus a paper roller make a typewriter, not a press or a telegraph.
Remember: identify the object from its visible parts, then ask what it was used for.
